newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian budget talks start, focus on pensions.
newsitem.headline: Italian budget talks start, focus on pensions.

text.p: Party leaders who support Italy's centre-left government met Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Monday to discuss the forthcoming 1997 budget, with the focus on proposed cuts in health and pension spending.

The government intends to unveil its budget at the end of the week, but newspapers said on Monday there was deadlock between Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and the hard left Communist Refoundation over welfare payments.
The package aims to cut 32.4 trillion lire off next year's deficit, but analysts are sceptical that this target can be met without action on pensions and health spending.
Ciampi was reported to be pressing for a one percent tax on pensions of people who had taken early retirement along with a general six month block on people seeking retirement.

Newspapers also quoted the state auditor's office as saying that proposals put forward by Health Minister Rosi Bindi for the budget would save just 1.2 trillion lire and not the 2.5 trillion lire called for.

Going into Monday's meeting, Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti told reporters he was against cuts in welfare spending. "Health and pensions cannot be hit yet again. On this we have no intention of giving way," he said.
The government controls the upper house of parliament (Senate), but relies on the support of the Refoundation to control the lower house of parliament.
Ciampi's drive for a tougher budget is linked to the planned creation of a single European currency in 1999.

At present Italy fails to meet any of the criteria established by the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to sign up for the Euro and a weak budget would put the country even further behind in its bid to meet the Maastricht terms.
Coalition party, the centrist Popular Party (PP), said on Monday it was in favour of a special "Maastricht tax" to help Italy prepare for the single currency.

PP leader Gerardo Bianco told reporters he was hopeful a deal could be struck with Refoundation. "We can find a solution, but the priority remains the entry into Europe and for this we might talk about a tax for Europe," he said.
